intro: This clinic mixes the contractions of spoken Japanese with their full forms. Every spoken form is just a longer phrase said fast, so the choice is never about sound alone: first decide which grammar is meant, then how it shortens, then whether the situation allows shortening at all. Ask the questions below in order.

skills.rule: Rebuild the full form, pick it by meaning, voice it if the te-form ends in で, and contract only when talking to friends or family.
skills.explain:
Q1. What is the full form? ている → てる, ておく → とく, てしまう → ちゃう, なければ → なきゃ, なくては → なくちゃ, ては → ちゃ, のだ → んだ, と / という / は → って, ところ → とこ, らない → んない.

Q2. What does the speaker mean? A state or an action in progress is てる. Something done in advance, ready for later, is とく. Something finished, often with regret, is ちゃう. An obligation is なきゃ or なくちゃ (both mean 'must' and are interchangeable). A ban is ちゃ or じゃ followed by だめ or いけない.

Q3. Does the te-form end in で (読んで, 飲んで, 泳いで, 遊んで)? Then the contraction is voiced too: でる, どく, じゃう, じゃ. Verbs whose te-form ends in て keep てる, とく, ちゃう, ちゃ.

Q4. Who is listening? Friends, family, yourself: contracted forms are normal. A boss, a customer, a meeting or anything written: use the full form even though the meaning is the same. The one contraction common in everyday polite speech is てます (見てます); in careful speech and writing, say ています.
patterns: state / in progress: ている → てる (でいる → でる)
in advance: ておく → とく (でおく → どく)
finished, regret: てしまう → ちゃう (でしまう → じゃう)
must: なければ → なきゃ, なくては → なくちゃ
must not: ては → ちゃ, では → じゃ + だめ
quote or topic: と / という / は → って

examples.jp: 今[いま]、テレビを見[み]{てる}。
もう遅[おそ]いから、帰[かえ]ら{なきゃ}。
examples.en: It's late, so I have to go home.

examples.jp: ケーキ、全部[ぜんぶ]食[た]べ{ちゃった}。
飲[の]み物[もの]は冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に入[い]れ{とく}ね。
examples.en: I'll put the drinks in the fridge so they're ready.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さん{って}、どんな人[ひと]？
部長[ぶちょう]、会議[かいぎ]の資料[しりょう]はもう準備[じゅんび]し{ておきました}。
examples.en: (To the department head) I've already prepared the materials for the meeting.

contrast.note: てる (ている) describes how things are now: 窓を開けてる, I've got the window open. とく (ておく) is a preparation for later: 窓を開けとく, I'll open the window (so the room airs).
ちゃう is てしまう, finished or regretted: 忘れちゃう. ちゃ is ては and is followed by だめ, いけない or 困る: 忘れちゃだめ, you mustn't forget.

contrast.vs: なきゃ vs ちゃだめ
contrast.note: なきゃ comes from a negative and means you must do it: 行かなきゃ. ちゃだめ means you must not: 行っちゃだめ. The negative な before きゃ is the giveaway.

mistakes.bad: 友達[ともだち]のジュースを飲[の]ん{ちゃった}。
mistakes.good: 友達[ともだち]のジュースを飲[の]ん{じゃった}。
mistakes.note: The te-form is 飲んで, so てしまった becomes じゃった, not ちゃった.

mistakes.bad: 授業[じゅぎょう]に遅[おく]れ{なきゃ}だめだよ。
mistakes.good: 授業[じゅぎょう]に遅[おく]れ{ちゃ}だめだよ。
mistakes.note: A ban is ては + だめ, which contracts to ちゃだめ. なきゃ would mean you have to be late.

mistakes.bad: 部長[ぶちょう]、資料[しりょう]をコピーし{ときました}。
mistakes.good: 部長[ぶちょう]、資料[しりょう]をコピーし{ておきました}。
mistakes.note: To a boss, use the full form ておきました; contractions belong to casual speech.

skills.tip: Say the full form in your head first; the contraction is that phrase said fast, and if the te-form has で, the contraction has a voiced sound too.
